answer.exemplar: A reflection is a flip and a rotation is a turn, and neither one changes the distance between any two points of the figure. Reflecting a segment places a segment of exactly the same length on the other side of the mirror line, and rotating a segment swings it through an angle without stretching it, so composing the two still leaves every corresponding pair of points exactly as far apart as it started. A composition built this way is therefore itself a rigid motion, and a rigid motion of the plane is one of four things: a translation, a rotation, a reflection, or a glide reflection. A dilation is the exception, because it multiplies every distance by the scale factor, so a composition including one does change the sizes involved.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to argue from the lengths of segments rather than assert the conclusion, since the conclusion only follows once length preservation is established.
questions.hint: Check what happens to the length of a single segment under each step.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a composition of rigid transformations preserves lengths

answer.exemplar: An arrangement such as an order of finishers records a sequence, and exchanging two finishers produces a different result because the positions themselves are the outcome, so each position is filled in turn and the counts multiply. A committee records only a set, and exchanging two members leaves the committee unchanged, so the same group has already been described once for every ordering of its members. The formula has to undo exactly that overcounting, which is why the count for a combination divides by the factorial of the number chosen while the count for a permutation does not. The test that separates the two situations is whether swapping two of the chosen items changes the answer.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to account for the overcounting that the division removes, rather than only listing the two formulas side by side.
questions.hint: Ask whether exchanging two chosen items changes the outcome.
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between ordered and unordered counting

questions.explanation: The reported point (5, 2) is exactly the reflection of (2, 5) over the line y = x, so the second step was skipped. A counterclockwise quarter turn maps (x, y) to (negative y, x), and applying it to (5, 2) gives (negative 2, 5), which is the correct final image. Rotations about the origin are defined for every point, and the order was fixed by the question rather than left open.
questions.hint: Work out what the reported point corresponds to, and then check the step that is missing.
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a skipped step in a transformation sequence
